extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency practitioners, and students of administrative law
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and recommended procedures for when and why courts should defer to agency statutory interpretations (Chevron v. Mead context), and how agencies can make adjudications worthy of deference. Focuses on delegation, expertise, accountability, formality, notice, and unfair-surprise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mead factors (care, consistency, formality, expertness, persuasiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have 'looked to the degree of the agency’s care, its consistency, formality, and relative expertness, and to the persuasiveness of the agency’s position' to determine whether an interpretation is worthy of deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the multi-factor, totality-of-the-circumstances indicators (Mead) that guide whether an interpretation merits Chevron-level deference; courts weigh thoroughness of consideration, validity of reasoning, consistency with earlier/later pronouncements, formality of the process, and the agency's relative expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal force requirement for Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will grant Chevron deference only to those interpretations with 'legal force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations produced by actions that have legal force (e.g., notice-and-comment rulemaking or formal adjudication) are the clearest candidates for Chevron deference; informal opinions or letter rulings are less likely to have legal force and thus less likely to receive Chevron treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation (Congressional intent to delegate interpretive authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should not give deference to an agency when Congress has not intended for the agency to fill in gaps; delegation is whether Congress intended courts or agencies to interpret the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of delegation looks to statutory indicators and historical practices. Barnhart factors inform this inquiry (see separate entry). Express congressional authorization to engage in rulemaking or adjudication is a 'very good indicator' of delegation meriting Chevron treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barnhart delegation factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether Congress intended to delegate, courts consider 'the interstitial nature of the legal question, the related expertise of the Agency, the importance of the question to administration of the statute, the complexity of that administration, and the careful consideration the Agency has given the question over a long period of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specific touchstones when assessing whether a particular statutory question is one Congress intended agencies (rather than courts) to resolve; long-standing agency consideration, technical interstitial issues, and high administrative complexity favor finding delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and demonstration thereof
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron rationales rest in part on agencies' 'technical expertise' that courts lack; agencies must demonstrate particularized expertise to be 'authoritative interpreters' of a statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies demonstrate expertise by explaining analyses and rationales in opinions or preambles; courts look to such explanations (as in notice-and-comment preambles) and to the factual analysis in adjudicatory opinions. Failure to explain can lead to reversal or lower deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore persuasiveness factors (thoroughness, validity, consistency, power to persuade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without Chevron deference, an agency's interpretation may have the 'power to persuade' under Skidmore based on 'the thoroughness evident in [an agency's] consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and all those factors which give it power to persuade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Chevron is not warranted, courts apply Skidmore-style review and weigh these persuasiveness factors to decide how much weight to afford the agency view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability / outside input (public participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accountability encompasses allowing agencies to receive information from non-agency parties; processes that permit outside input expand information available to agencies and can make policy more legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice-and-comment rulemaking exemplifies this accountability by requiring solicitation and response to public input. For adjudications, agencies can solicit amicus briefs, permit intervention, or otherwise open adjudicatory proceedings to nonparties; courts may view policies developed with outside input as more legitimate and more deserving of deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of comment opportunities for policy-changing adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications lack an APA requirement to publish notice as rulemakings do, but agencies could place notices in the Federal Register or otherwise publicize adjudications likely to be precedent-setting and solicit amicus briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should (optionally) publish notices describing issues, link to dockets/filings, permit submissions via regs.gov, and improve docketing systems so the public can view and submit amicus briefs—mirroring appeals-court practices—to provide equivalent notice and participation opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and explanation of new policies (responding to comments and publicizing holdings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking benefits include explaining agencies' rationales and responding to public comments; adjudications may not address amici arguments or be as widely published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies seeking deference for adjudicative policies should respond on the record to material amici comments, publish precedential decisions (with summaries), issue guidance/press releases, and compile adjudicative holdings—so courts can see the agency's deliberation and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality and procedural safeguards (quality over APA dichotomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consideration of how adjudications comport with Chevron should rely on the quality of procedural safeguards offered during an adjudication, rather than the APA's formal/informal dichotomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some 'informal' adjudications provide more procedural protections than some 'formal' ones; agencies' organic statutes or rules of procedure can supply safeguards (on-the-record hearings, evidentiary protections) that strengthen claims to deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unfair surprise / fair warning principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental rule-of-law principle requires that those subject to law must have a reasonable opportunity to know what is prohibited; courts guard against agency actions that cause 'unfair surprise' by retroactively imposing new policy standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicative policymaking is permissible so long as it does not produce unfair surprise—courts have long refused to apply new agency positions retroactively to conduct taken in reliance on prior law. When an agency changes precedent, courts may limit retrospective application but apply the new policy prospectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express congressional authorization as an indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Mead recognized that 'express congressional authorizations to engage in the rulemaking or adjudication that produces regulations or rulings for which deference is claimed' are strong indicators that Congress intended delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statutes explicitly authorize particular procedural mechanisms or decisionmaking power, courts are likelier to treat resulting agency interpretations as entitled to Chevron deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural reforms to make adjudication comparable to rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can take specific steps to ensure adjudications provide the same demonstrations of expertise, public input, and notice that rulemaking does, thus making adjudicative policymaking more defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended measures include: accepting amicus briefs broadly; permitting intervention where suitable; publishing Federal Register notices for significant adjudications; using public dockets and regs.gov for submissions; responding on the record to material amici comments; publicizing precedential decisions and providing summaries; and compiling adjudicative holdings for public access.
